meta.name: The Great Rift
meta.author: Hu Qian · adapted from the novella 大裂
meta.description: A branching visual novel adapted from Hu Qian’s novella 大裂. Dialogue and narration are rewritten and translated, not the original text. For personal study only; confirm adaptation rights before publishing.

assets.name: Background · The mound in the dream

variables.name: Charged in on the seventh night

commands.text: — 1 · The Seventh Night —
Nobody ever wanted to talk much about that night afterwards. It happened on the seventh night in a row that we'd been playing cards.
Six people, four decks, everyone clutching a stack as thick as a dictionary. I suspect whoever invented the game hated time and wanted it to die noisily.
There were several tricks to it, but really only one: make the player before you die with his cards still in his hand.
The player before me was always Ding Weiyang. He learned slowly; I learned fast. It was the first time in five years I'd learned anything faster than anyone else.
Liu Qingqing was sorting his cards and trying not to laugh.
Couple of days ago at the internet café, some guy wouldn't give up his seat to the Old Guard.
Why should he?
That's what he said. So the Old Guard guy points right at his nose — "Just you wait. We'll cut you to pieces. Not a scrap of armour left."
"Not a scrap of armour"? Those were his words?

Liu Qingqing nodded, laughing so hard he could barely hold his cards. We all collapsed. Even the dorm head, sitting off to one side writing our "bad conduct" in his notebook, twitched at the corner of his mouth.
Not a scrap of armour left. We agreed it was the funniest thing any of us had heard that year.
One in the morning, last hand. Once again I left Ding Weiyang dead with his cards in his hand.
He held his half-played hand and looked around blankly, like a student hearing the bell at the end of an exam. Then he put the cards down gently and went out.
We all thought he'd just gone to wash his face.
A roar burst out in the corridor.
It was long and hoarse, and it bounced back and forth across that wasteland the city had thrown away. It was a long time before I understood: it was the sound an animal makes just before it dies.
A clatter of feet came from downstairs.
Ding Weiyang crashed back through the door and pressed his back hard against it. His thick tongue got thicker when he panicked.
They're… coming up.
Before he'd finished, a beer bottle exploded outside and broken glass slid in under the door.
I think… they've got knives.

It was the Old Guard: the year above us, a hundred or so of them, on the second floor. We were the first intake since the school changed its name, living on the third and fourth. To them, we'd come to take their ground.
The sound of doors being kicked in moved towards us, one room at a time. Metal hitting bed frames, hitting lockers, hitting people.

options.text: Wedge a chair against the door
Grab the mop from the corner and stand next to Ding Weiyang
Shrink into the corner and hold your breath

commands.prompt: The noise outside is getting closer.

commands.text: A deep voice suddenly rang out at the end of the corridor: "Everybody out! There's more of us than them! Don't be scared!"
For a moment, the Old Guard actually went quiet.
Someone in our room whispered: open the door.
Ding Weiyang's hand was on the handle, his chest rising and falling.
The door opened. Here and there along the corridor, other doors opened too. Guo Zhonghan took a pair of scissors from his drawer and gripped them until his knuckles went white.
Then a dull thud. The man who'd shouted went down in the corridor under a single blow.
Since the doors were open anyway, the Old Guard saved themselves the kicking. They came in threes and fours and swung at whoever they saw.
Our door was kicked wide. Ding Weiyang was thrown out, hit his forehead on the tiles, and didn't move.
Who opened the door?
Nobody spoke. The dorm head shrank into his chair, raised one crooked finger, and pointed at Ding Weiyang on the floor.
An iron bar came down on Ding Weiyang's shoulder blade. Several feet took turns stamping. He tried to push himself up and was stamped down; tried again, and was stamped down again.
A line of red slowly spread out from under his head.

commands.prompt: A dozen heads crowd the doorway.

commands.text: I hadn't got past the threshold before something hit my stomach, then my head.
It didn't hurt. I was just dizzy, rings of dizziness spreading through my skull, and I slid down the door frame.
Before I went down, my eyes met Ding Weiyang's on the floor. His face was covered in blood, but he seemed to see clearly who had come at them.
Then Zhao Naifu threw himself out of the corner with a yell that seemed to burst from his chest. He went down too, the corner of his eye split open.
I reached out, then pulled my hand back.
"I can't beat them." I said it to myself again and again. It was true, and it didn't make me feel any better.
Zhao Naifu yelled in the corner and charged out. Three bars came down on him at once. When he fell, the corner of his eye split open.
I stood where I was and didn't take a single blow. Later I learned that not taking a single blow was the hardest thing to take that night.
Around three, the Old Guard went back down to the second floor.

The corridor was a slaughterhouse, broken glass and blood all the way along. Everyone who'd been beaten stayed in their rooms. Nobody spoke and nobody moved, like a room full of appliances with the plugs pulled.
Ding Weiyang was helped into a chair. The nosebleed had dried on his neck in patches, like fish scales. The dorm head kept his back to everyone, rubbing that crooked finger until it swelled.
Just before dawn, I climbed up to the roof.
The fat guy who'd shouted "Everybody out" was lying face down up there, one arm twisted at an angle no arm should have. His cheek was against the concrete; I couldn't tell if he was still breathing.
Five in the morning, and the cold had wrapped the whole wasteland up tight.
Maybe it was that morning when we started deciding to believe in a treasure map.
— 2 · How Everyone Got Here —
Let me go back. My middle school and my high school were both the worst in the city. The city had over a million young people, and I always felt I was in the most hopeless five percent of them.

I sat the film academy entrance exams for five years. The first year I got a pass certificate from the best school and walked on air; then the number of candidates in the province hit a record, the cut-off rose with it, and I was dropped.
For the next four years I'd work out my rank among hundreds of thousands of candidates, like a patient taking his temperature every day and finding himself colder each time.

In the second year my father caught me watching a disc of doubtful origin in my room, and decided from then on that "studying film" meant shutting the door and doing nothing useful. That was also the year I met Zhao Naifu, in a basement in Beijing.
In the fifth year I started losing my hair and got my worst score in five years. My father said if I failed again, he'd pull some strings and get me a job driving a sanitation truck.
My mother hadn't said much for a long time. That day, she handed me an admissions brochure.
Have a look at this.

commands.prompt: Down the edge of the cover, a school's name is printed in a column, trying hard to look respectable.

commands.text: I'd rather drive the garbage truck.
My mother didn't say anything else. She turned away. I saw the white hair at her temples, and her shoulders, which wouldn't stop shaking.
I stood there a while. Then I took the brochure after all.
The day I left, I shouldered the travel bag I'd used for five years, with more compartments than a maze, and said to my mother:
Even at a school like that, I'll fight my way out.
Then I cried. The first time in five years.
My father kicked over the marble coffee table that had stood in our living room for twenty years. That was his send-off.
The edge of the city: a dead-straight highway, and on both sides, wasteland as far as you could see. Once autumn came, the earth turned an irritable yellow.

It used to be called the Broadcasting Institute. After it expanded it was renamed Shanhua College of Communication, and everyone called it Shanchuan. The teaching block was a converted chemical plant. If you lined up all three hundred-odd vocational colleges in the country, it would be at the very back, in charge of turning off the lights.
On registration day, all the new students stood in the little square in front of the canteen, each holding the same thin plastic basin and the same straw-filled quilt.
The sky was overcast and nobody spoke. We all stared at the canteen's greasy double doors and slowly understood one thing: this was it. We were done for.
From the second-floor windows of the dorm block, the Old Guard leaned on the sills peeling bananas and watched us. They weren't waiting for anything. They just felt we'd crowded into their place.
In the corridor I ran into Guo Zhonghan, who'd sat next to me in the repeat-year class. I thought he'd gone to Shanghai. From the look of it, so had he.
Guo Zhonghan was big and tall, with a baby face. To look older he'd grown a beard, but the beard wouldn't grow either; it looked like the film that forms on a steamed bun left out too long.
I choked in the exam. Five points short. My girlfriend's already in Shanghai. Look — Hongqiao.
He shoved a photo on his phone in my face. Given how much he slept in the repeat class, five points short was the heavens being generous.

In the bed across from his was Liu Qingqing: round head, dark skin, lying there while his dad put the pillowcase on for him. His dad was as thin as a stick of firewood. He didn't say a word, just grunted, and dragged him off to the canteen.
Then someone appeared behind us.
Thick eyebrows, big eyes, a checked shirt without a single crease, like someone who'd walked off the wrong set of a nineties comic.
Hello. My name's Ding Weiyang.

When he spoke, it was as if a few rays of sunlight had come into the room. He didn't belong here at all. By Shanchuan standards, everyone was supposed to have dead-fish eyes and mud on their trouser cuffs.
Ding Weiyang bent to unzip his suitcase. Guo Zhonghan, passing, slapped him on the backside. Ding Weiyang turned round and gave him a brilliant smile.
I slapped him too. He smiled at me as well.
Guo Zhonghan was already at the door when he came back and slapped him again. This time Ding Weiyang finally froze.
…What are you doing?
The friendship between the three of us was founded on one man reacting two beats late.
Guo Zhonghan sat backwards on a chair, chin on the backrest, looking at me.
And you? How'd you end up here?

options.text: Tell the truth: five years of exams, never got in

commands.text: Guo Zhonghan nodded. It was the kind of nod that made you want to kick his chair over.

On my locker door, someone before me had copied out a few lines of the Bible in careful, childish handwriting, something about the earth being filled with violence and all flesh being corrupt. Underneath, someone else had added a line of swearing, by way of a book review.
That evening in the canteen, a girl slipped while carrying her tray and tipped a plate of fish-fragrant aubergine all over herself. She sat on the floor, gazing into the distance, puzzled.
Everyone looked up and gazed at her, puzzled. Nobody knew what was happening.
— 3 · Gathering —
In the first two weeks of term, the first thing the new students accomplished was knocking through a wall.

A fat guy wanted to get to the west side of campus, but the only gate was on the east. He remembered he'd learned to drive an excavator at technical school, and there happened to be one parked on the building site.
He climbed in and pushed a hole through the wall. The people watching applauded. From then on he was known as Lord Westgate.
Later he laid a pebble path overnight, straight from the west gate to the internet café. It was the only infrastructure project our year ever completed.
It was him who shouted "Everybody out" that night, and got flattened like a pancake on the roof.
Around then I kept having the same dream.
A mound of earth about three metres high, covered in snow-white silkie chickens. They climbed up it, and climbed back down.
I crouched there watching them, and I was happy. I thought: this must be my own little universe.
On the second day of term, Liu Qingqing wanted to tear a page out of Ding Weiyang's notebook.
No. That paper's for studying.
The whole class went silent, as if someone had told a joke at a funeral.
Studying what?
He ripped the page out. Ding Weiyang went red and crouched down. I thought he was looking for a brick — instead he pulled the chair out from under Liu Qingqing.
Liu Qingqing slid under the desk and didn't come up for a long time. The teacher stood on tiptoe, had a look, and went on with the lesson.
When he surfaced again he was at the other end of the classroom, holding a dustpan in each hand, sweating, panting at every step, as if he'd run a marathon before going to war.
Guo Zhonghan stood up and pushed them both back into their seats.
Enough. Both of you. Studying isn't sacred — if it were, why would you be here?
Ding Weiyang was so comforted his eyes went red. Later I asked Liu Qingqing why he'd needed that page so badly. He said he'd thought of a joke and wanted to write it down.
Didn't get to write it down. Forgot it.

From then on Ding Weiyang decided to write essays in his notebook. But he would always write one sentence and never manage another. I leaned over to look. The whole page had a single line on it, no punctuation:
Today I am very happy
If you write it like that, you can't go on.
Then what should I write?
I had no answer. That cartoonish light in his eyes made me a little afraid to look.
Fewer people came to class each day. In the end each classroom had only one person in it, and they took turns.
The Old Guard started picking on the new students. One of them, Yang Bang, got into a fight over a toilet cubicle and was pushed head first into the latrine.
Guo Zhonghan and I decided to start a film club.
Get a bunch of people together, maybe we can do something.

I drew the poster several times in charcoal, copying the cover of a book: a documentary director leading his crew along a ridge between fields. The book was about how walking the same field once and walking it for ten years show you different things.

The next day, our posters were all covered by the roller-skating club's. So we changed the meeting place on their posters to ours. It was the first thing the film club ever accomplished, and very nearly the last.
On recruitment day, someone turned up with soap suds still in his hair.
The Old Guard cut off the water in the bathhouse. Threw our towels away too.
I handed him a new blackboard eraser. He stood at the window facing the wasteland and rubbed his hair with it, stroke by stroke.
I'm Li Ning.
Towards evening, Zhao Naifu came too. He was as surprised to see me as I was to see him.
I didn't want to die in my hometown.

He was from Mudanjiang, two thousand kilometres away. He lived in the only new students' room that had been put on the second floor, and every day the Old Guard piled rubbish outside his door. His body had been made for a basketball court; his mind seemed to have been made for another, slower world.
The film club signed up five people. Besides Li Ning and Zhao Naifu, there were two girls: Wang Ziye, small, quick, with curly hair, and Liang Xiao, who looked a little dazed.
I've got a bad feeling about this.
Every time he said that, something good happened to him next. This time the good thing was that he got to sit next to Wang Ziye.
The first meeting was on the sports field. Nobody knew what to do.
Li Ning took a crumpled sheet of paper from inside his jacket. It had been torn out of Ding Weiyang's notebook.
This was my favourite story before I came to college. Could you all have a look?
The page went round. The story was about a son who accidentally turned into a pig. His father didn't mind at all, and the family actually got along better because of it.
Nobody said anything. When the page reached Liang Xiao, she stared at it for a long time.
…It's really well written.
Li Ning looked at us. The page came to me last.

options.text: Read it properly and tell him what you really think

then.text: The less his dad minds, the worse it feels to read. Is that what you meant to write?
Li Ning was taken aback. His eyes lit up for a moment, then went dark again.
…More or less.
He folded the page and put it back inside his jacket. The others were already on their feet.

else.text: I handed the page back. Li Ning took it and folded it in four.

commands.text: Zhao Naifu spotted a basketball in the corner of the field.
Let's shoot some hoops.
Everyone breathed out. Zhao Naifu told me later that the feeling of "pouring out your sweat to your heart's content" was unbelievably fake.
We'd barely warmed up when a dozen of the Old Guard surrounded us. A shirtless guy with a crew cut tucked the ball under his arm.
This time slot's ours. Don't like it? Keep playing. Go on, I dare you.
The crew cut grinned and slammed the ball at us. In the end it was Wang Ziye and Liang Xiao who pulled everyone away.
That was the film club's one and only meeting.
A few days later I ran into Li Ning outside the bathhouse again. He was standing in the cold wind with wet hair, and no towel.
That day Liang Xiao said "it's really well written". What do you think she meant?

then.text: I think she honestly didn't know what to say.
At least you read it to the end.
The way he said it didn't sound like thanks. It sounded like he was keeping accounts.

else.text: I said I hadn't really read it. Li Ning nodded, as if that was exactly the answer he wanted.

commands.text: I'm not going to wipe it off any more.
I didn't understand. It was a long time before I realised he wasn't talking about the soap in his hair.
Later, Wang Ziye pushed a camera with a long zoom lens into my hands. She said she'd borrowed it in the club's name from the Old Guard on the second floor.
It's time to give it back. I heard it's pretty dangerous down there… Would you go?
She blinked when she said "dangerous", as if it were something adorable. I took the camera and left before I could say anything.
For the first time I crossed the line and went onto the second floor. There was a mountain of rubbish outside every door, and the smell hit you like a hammer.

The door of that room was half open. Inside it was dark as a cellar. Four people were sprawled on their beds in various positions; you couldn't tell if they were still breathing. The floor was sticky.
Cui Chen?
The mosquito net in the corner swayed, and a cough came from inside.
…Huh?
Your camera. I'll leave it here.
He struggled to sit up, then, as if he'd used up a whole day's strength, lay back down.
Oh. OK.
I escaped. That room came back to me in dreams again and again.
I've always felt it was the place our whole generation lives in, only painted a different colour.
— 4 · Gold —

Before that night, Guo Zhonghan and Wang Ziye had dug a small plot south of the school to grow "peonies". He'd bought the seeds from someone he'd flagged down by the highway. They were actually jasmine; he never found out.
A week went by. The weeds around it grew beautifully. Nothing grew in his plot.
Do you think the soil digested the seeds?
Seeds have to be soaked first. …In fertiliser water.
I know. I just forgot.
In his agricultural knowledge, fertiliser meant manure. He really did soak the seeds in manure water. More incredible still, they really did sprout.

Wang Ziye crouched beside the plot, poking the earth with a little stick. The two of them looked at that row of shoots like a pair of farmers who'd just been given their first field. It was the closest thing to happiness I ever saw at Shanchuan, if a little smelly.
But no sooner had the shoots come up than someone cut them off at the root in the night.
One night Liu Qingqing and I were coming back from the internet café when we caught a figure snipping at the buds with a pair of scissors.
Don't move!
The figure didn't turn round. It shot off into the dark like a gust of wind.
Only later did I realise it was Liang Xiao. Later still, I saw her crouching alone by the dead stems, taping little yellow flowers back on, one by one.
I didn't go over. She wanted to do these things in secret, whether they were bad things or good things nobody needed.
After the violence, the school put two doors between the second and third floors. The badly hurt went home to the city; everyone else lay in their dorms.
The school said anyone who told their parents would be expelled. Most of the new students didn't want to tell anyway — if it got out, it would get in the way of their revenge.

The idea of revenge had sprouted everywhere the moment the Old Guard withdrew to the second floor, and it grew a lot faster than Guo Zhonghan's jasmine. Yang Bang got hold of several hundred kilos of steel pipe.
Once Zhao Naifu could get out of bed, I took him walking into the wasteland. North, south, east, west: land as far as you could see.
I had a feeling my life was about to be turned completely over. Somewhere out there, an entrance was hidden.
Walking east, we found a low hut with no windows, full of hay and dung.
I sat down to rest on a big rock beside the hut, and suddenly heard a rustling, as if something had crawled past me and gone into the ground.
I stood up and stared at the rock. Not far off there were two more just like it. Three rocks standing on the wasteland, like three people who refused to talk.
What's wrong?
There's something under here. I heard it.
Rats, probably. It's getting dark.

options.text: Heave it over with Zhao Naifu

commands.prompt: The rock is heavy. The sun is nearly down.

commands.text: We pushed together, and the rock rolled over, showing the side that hadn't seen light for who knows how many years.
In the hollow underneath lay a plank that had almost rotted away. Up close, I could make out a line of crooked words carved into it:
You will have no father and no mother, and no one to lean on.
In the cold wind, neither of us could speak. I turned to look at Zhao Naifu. The gauze covered half of one eye; the half that showed was full of tears.
Let's dig.
Yeah. …I heard it too.
We found flat stones and scraped downwards. The ground was hard; each stroke took off only a thin layer. Half a metre down it was fully dark, and we dug out a piece of leather folded into a square.
We shook off the dirt and the millipedes and opened it. It was a map, carved into the hide: the coal hill to the west, the village to the north, and this hut to the east as the starting point.
Somewhere to the south there was a mark. Next to it, one word was carved: GOLD.
I knew it was very likely a joke. But if anything in our lives could still change, the entrance had to be here.
Neither of us said a word on the way back. When we were nearly at the dorm block, I asked him:
Do we tell them?
There's strength in numbers.

options.text: Tell the people in the dorm

commands.text: Guo Zhonghan, on crutches, was sitting at the computer playing a game he wouldn't want anyone to see, plasters on his fingers where the mouse had raised blisters. Ding Weiyang was lying facing the wall; he'd been lying like that for days. In the corner were six steel pipes another dorm had sent over.
I've found gold.
Nobody paid any attention. Zhao Naifu spread out the map, and the room filled with a smell of rot.
What's that stink?
Guo Zhonghan glanced back, then turned away again.
Gold! Here's your gold!
He grabbed his crutch and threw it at me. Ding Weiyang roared at the wall:
Get lost! Let me lie here!
As Zhao Naifu went back down to the second floor, he said on the stairs:
Everyone in this building is already dead.
We didn't turn the rock over.
On the way back, Zhao Naifu said we'd come again next time. Neither of us ever went back.
Later, on the night of the revenge, I locked myself in the dorm, put my headphones on, and waited until it was light.
Three years after that I got a diploma nobody cared about and went back to the city.
The man my father had pulled strings with was still there. I put on the orange uniform, sat up high in the cab of the sanitation truck, and drove back and forth over the potholed roads.
I'd finally worked out my position. I didn't need to work it out any more.
Sometimes I wind down the window and spit outside.
Now and then I dream about that wasteland, that hut, and the three identical rocks.
In the dream I always crouch down and put my palms against the cold stone, and I can never find the strength to push.
【Ending: The Last Five Percent】
— 5 · The Cave —
I measured the map's scale and fixed the mark south of the school, behind a mound so desolate even the excavators didn't go there.
At first it felt like a game. When I woke up the next day I understood: it was no different from Guo Zhonghan growing flowers or Lord Westgate laying his path. I'd just finally found something to do.
Three days of digging turned up nothing but dirt.
Zhao Naifu didn't think much of the shovel, so he "borrowed" a pickaxe from the village to the north.
The villagers carve a mark on all their tools, and neighbours don't steal from each other. So they're really easy to steal.
I took the pickaxe. On the wooden handle was a crooked circle with a dot in the middle, like an eye that couldn't close.
I wanted an iron bucket to carry the earth, so I went to the village. In the hardware store, the owner patted the last one in the corner.
That's the only one left. Students from your school keep coming in for iron buckets lately, several at a time. What do you need all those buckets for, a water fight?
I didn't know either. At the time I just thought I was unlucky.
There was a middle-aged man in the shop too, buying a pickaxe.
Lost the pickaxe at home again. Last time it was the shovel.
How do you lose one of those? Everybody's got one.
…You've got the most.
I stood to one side, pretending to study the size of the bucket, feeling rotten. I bought a whole box of candles while I was at it.
On the way back the man said he lived just up ahead. Outside his gate stood a wheelbarrow. On its handle was the same eye that couldn't close.
It was getting dark. I set the box of candles gently down at his gate and wheeled the barrow away. As if swapping a box of candles for a barrow didn't count as stealing.
Zhao Naifu was sitting by the pit, covered in dust, smoking. When he saw the barrow, he grinned, showing a mouthful of white teeth.
That barrow… isn't from that house, is it?
Another day's digging, and still only dirt. The sun was going down in the west. I looked at the mud all over my hands.
Forget it. It's all fake.
Zhao Naifu climbed out of the pit, the scar by his eye still red.
No. I believe it.
That night, a storm broke.
Zhao Naifu burst into our room.
We piled the dirt too close to the hole! In rain like this it'll wash back in and fill the whole thing up!
He grabbed an umbrella from the corner.

options.text: Run out into the rain with him

commands.prompt: Rain mixed with sleet hammers on the window.

commands.text: We stumbled south through the mud. The mound had collapsed and the pit was buried completely.
Zhao Naifu knelt in the mud and dug with his hands. After two handfuls he stopped.
The two of us stood in the rain like a pair of drowned dogs. Neither of us said anything about going back.
Zhao Naifu ran out alone. In the middle of the night he came back, streaming with water, and stood in the corridor.
It's gone. The mound collapsed. The pit's buried.
Then stop digging. Throw the map away. We're a joke.
No! There'll be gold.
Can you dig a thousand metres? Can you dig for five years?
Even I hadn't expected to be that cruel. He looked at me.
You don't understand.
It rained for two nights. On the third morning it stopped.
The mound was gone. All that was left was a soggy hollow. Zhao Naifu crouched there as if someone in his family had died.
I thought of the dream. A mound of earth, a flock of white silkie chickens.
Suddenly I understood.
You idiot! That little hole we dug couldn't swallow a whole mound.
…So what?
It's hollow underneath!
He thought about it for a full five seconds before he said "Oh." In those five seconds I felt a little proud on behalf of heaven: it had finally given me a brain that worked.

The mud was loose; every spadeful came away in a big chunk. Before noon, an opening more than a metre high had appeared under the mound, sloping down, breathing out a smell of rainwater and rotten leaves.
Gold shines, right?
Only if there's light. Where are the candles?
I was scared they'd get wet. I took them back to the dorm.
How can candles get wet?
He ran back for them. I couldn't wait. I grabbed the lighter he'd left behind and crawled in alone.
The hole was only three metres deep. I'd been fooled again.
As I shuffled back, my foot came down on something hard. The lighter got too hot to hold and went out.
Strangely, I wasn't afraid. There was an indescribable calm in the dark, as if the whole wasteland had been shut outside.
When I lit it again, I saw clearly: a thigh bone, still attached to a length of shin that disappeared into the earth.
I crawled out. Zhao Naifu came running back with the candles and looked at me.
You've been in. What's down there?
Zhao Naifu crawled in. When he came out he was holding up the thigh bone, wiping the dirt off with his sleeve.
Come on.

And so he carried a human bone right across campus and into Guo Zhonghan's room. Nobody on the way gave it a second look. At Shanchuan, someone walking around holding a bone wasn't any stranger than anything else.
Yang Bang was sitting in the middle of the room, a sidekick in glasses standing beside him. He spoke as if he were unveiling a bronze statue of himself.
Good, you're here too. I'll say it to all of you. We've got three more years in this place. If we don't hit back this time, they'll be shitting on our heads from now on.

Everything in this world has to be fought for. Even if there's only a little light, you grab it and you don't let go. I've come in person to invite all of you with ambition to join us and take this school.
Guo Zhonghan's eyelids drooped; he was nearly asleep. But Ding Weiyang had twisted round on his bed and was listening intently.
Look!
He held the thigh bone up in front of each of them. Ding Weiyang's face went white.
We've got a treasure map. We can dig up gold! We've already dug up this! Yang Bang, bring your people and dig with us. Once we find it, everything'll be different for all of us!
Yang Bang looked at him coldly.
Childish. A treasure map? Digging for gold? Do you live in a fairy tale? We're healing, we're preparing, and you're daydreaming.
He stood up and turned to me.
What about you? You don't seem like them.

commands.prompt: Yang Bang holds out his hand to you.

commands.text: Yang Bang snorted and left with Glasses.
Farewell, General.
Yang Bang didn't catch the sarcasm.
We're saved. We'll find the gold, get out of here, and go do everything in the world.
Everyone in the room except Liu Qingqing got down from their beds and chairs. The moment they stepped into the sun they shielded their eyes with their hands like vampires.
No, I'm going to burn to ash.
I followed Yang Bang out. Behind me, Zhao Naifu was still holding up the bone.
Yang Bang's meetings were held in the biggest classroom. A dozen-odd people sat around a row of pushed-together desks, backs very straight, like a crop of potatoes waiting for inspection.
Li Ning stood beside Yang Bang like a sidekick. Since the violence, he'd looked down on us "spineless" ones.
Don't you feel even a little ashamed?
After the meeting, Yang Bang cooked Western food himself. The stove burned coal briquettes and couldn't be brought into the classroom, so everyone squatted in the ground-floor hall to eat.
For a few days I felt alive again. Somebody was finally telling me what to do.
There are twice as many of us as the Old Guard. That night, once we've knocked them down, we go in pairs and carry every one of them out into the wasteland.
When they wake up, let them see themselves lying out in the fields like drowned corpses.
Everyone banged the table and cheered. I banged it too.
Wang Ziye started sitting next to Yang Bang. She watched him talk the way you'd look at a statue.
One day in the canteen, Guo Zhonghan came lurching over, smelling strange. He sat down next to Wang Ziye and grabbed Yang Bang's hand — he'd meant to grab Wang Ziye's.
Little Yang, do you think you're great? What makes you so pleased with yourself all the time?
The people around Yang Bang stood up. Yang Bang raised a hand and gestured for them to sit.
We'll talk when you've sobered up.
Guo Zhonghan raised his head and saw me. He froze for a moment, then laughed.
Oh. You're here too.

options.text: Get up and go and hold him up

commands.prompt: Guo Zhonghan slumps over the table. Nobody helps him.

commands.text: I got Guo Zhonghan's arm over my shoulder and helped him out of the canteen step by step. Behind me, not one of Yang Bang's people made a sound.
After that I never went to another meeting.
Ding Weiyang told me that in those days they'd dug a bundle of strange weed out of the cave, and that was what Guo Zhonghan had smoked.
— 6 · Salvia —
Ding Weiyang and Guo Zhonghan joined in. I drew them a map of the village and sent them to the hardware store for tools.
They never went into the store. Guo Zhonghan, knowing the way, led Ding Weiyang over the wall of that house.
That house again. I started to suspect it was the only bank on the whole wasteland.
Zhao Naifu and I went to the village to buy gloves, and outside the hardware store we ran into that man again. He looked like a rotten pear.
The pickaxe and the shovel are gone again. Young man, the world's getting worse and worse.

He talked a lot. Said he'd been to England, and wherever he went he lived next to a rubbish heap. Said what lay between people was decades, a hundred years, two hundred years. As he talked, he picked a white chicken feather out of his beard and looked at it between his fingers.
You can't stop the world getting worse. It's like a train going over a cliff, the carriages falling off one at a time. And this train is two hundred years long.
I don't expect anyone from your school to give my things back. I just want you to pass on a message: even if they do come back one day, nothing will get better because of it.
That's so hopeless.
It is. How much money have you got on you? …More than I had at your age. Good.
He wheeled a brand-new barrow home. We knew that direction far too well.
On the bus to town, Zhao Naifu was in a daze the whole way.
Why do we keep stealing from his house? …He got to me.
He didn't explain anything. He just lost some stuff and grumbled about it.
You don't understand.
When we got off, there was a row of KTV bars by the road. A woman was tapping on the glass.
Coming in? Come on!
Zhao Naifu stopped. I pulled at him; he shook my hand off, his face bright red.
I've been holding it in for years. You go buy the water jug.
We stuck candles all over the cave walls. The wax ran down the earth and set every metre or so in a ridge, like the marks on a ruler. At last we had something we could measure.
One day after work, Ding Weiyang handed me his notebook with an air of great mystery. Below "Today I am very happy" was a second line:
Today we dug one metre
He looked at me, his eyes shining as if they'd just been oiled.
I wrote a second sentence.
The hole went down six or seven metres. On the third day, Guo Zhonghan threw down his shovel.
What are we doing? We're wasting our lives. Our lives are rubbish, but if you sort through rubbish there's always something you can recycle. Digging this hole is setting fire to the whole heap.
I think I'm better than I was. I don't feel weak any more.
Guo Zhonghan burst out laughing and reached over to pinch Ding Weiyang's backside. Ding Weiyang didn't flinch and didn't care. That made Guo Zhonghan very unhappy.

options.text: Snap back: "You're a dog. One bit of effort and you're right back where you started."

commands.prompt: Guo Zhonghan's words get nastier and nastier.

commands.text: Guo Zhonghan turned and charged back into the hole. He swung the pickaxe like a madman, cursing us all as pieces of shit. A little over an hour later, a package came flying out of the hole.
Inside a hardened plastic sheet was a bag of long, dried leaves. Like tea, but with a much stronger smell.
Zhao Naifu squeezed the tobacco out of a cigarette, stuffed the leaves in, lit it, and took a deep drag. It went round the circle and reached me.

then.text: A few minutes later, everything around me started to swell. The little trees nearby grew outward like sponges, and the stars in the sky joined up into constellations I had never seen.
I thought of the bones. They seemed to be lying right in front of me, clean, glowing like white jade.

else.text: I passed it to Ding Weiyang. He didn't know how to smoke, so he steeped the leaves in his water bottle and gulped it down like herbal tea.
Clear-headed, I watched them collapse on the ground one by one, like a few dropped eggs.

commands.text: We went to the canteen to eat. Wang Ziye and Yang Bang were sitting not far away.
Guo Zhonghan stared at Wang Ziye for a long time, as if he'd only just remembered such a person existed. He lurched over and plonked himself down beside her.
Little Yang. Do you think you're great?
I wouldn't go that far.
"Wouldn't go that far." What makes you so pleased with yourself all the time? You don't even know how a piss works!
We'll talk when you've sobered up.
Wang Ziye, come on, come grow flowers with me. Water them with manure and they bloom.
Wang Ziye took Yang Bang's arm and stood up, and looked back at Guo Zhonghan with pity. That one look knocked him flat.
Guo Zhonghan lifted his face from the table and pulled his trench coat tight. Under the coat was a patched wool jumper; you'd never have known from the outside.
These people are hilarious.
Liu Qingqing recognised the weed: Mexican salvia. Zhao Naifu took it.

Later Liu Qingqing said he'd seen Zhao Naifu outside the internet café, hands in his pockets, asking passers-by, "Want some?" When they shook their heads, he'd say "Go on, then," and they'd come over. It was the shortest sales pitch I've ever seen.
When I went to his room, he was packing. His lips were purple.
Where are you going?
Into town. I mix the salvia into ordinary tobacco and sell it. It'll keep me going for a while.
What about the gold?
Don't want it.
He pushed a jumper into his bag. It took several tries to get it in.
The first week of term, one night playing cards, I had unreal luck. Both jokers in my hand all night. Remember?
I remembered. Ding Weiyang had been so happy for him that night he'd nearly cried.
I borrowed Li Ning's phone and went up to the roof to call her. Five years, and I finally had one good thing I could tell her.
She picked up. She asked who it was. I said, it's me.
Then she started screaming. Screamed and screamed, and hung up.
A thousand love letters, traded for a night of jokers, traded for a scream. From that day on I knew I was finished.
That day after the salvia, I'd never been so clear-headed. I saw how pitiful everyone is — you, Ding Weiyang, everyone. Gold can't change that.

then.text: You smoked it too. Didn't you feel clear?

commands.text: My whole life there's been a thick fog in front of me. These last few days, it suddenly lifted. I saw colours. Have you ever seen colours?

options.text: Quietly help him carry his bags

commands.prompt: He has packed two big bags.

commands.text: I carried his bags across the barren campus, out through the hole in the north wall, and stood with him by the highway.
When we find the gold, I'll call you.
Will I still need it? …I don't know.
The bus came. He pulled his dogskin jacket tight and got on. Only after it had gone did I find that he'd left the leather map in my bag.
Wang Ziye moved into Yang Bang's room. In the corridor, in the toilets, Guo Zhonghan could always hear her praising Yang Bang. He rolled around on the floor.
I'll move into the cave.
We dug out a space in the cave big enough for a steel camp bed and nailed plastic sheeting to the walls. The candlelight picked out the creases in the plastic, line by line.
In mid-November, Liang Xiao's family came to take her away and sent her abroad. The rumour around school was that Li Ning had raped her in the woods.
Before she left, she came to find me. Her lips were cracked, and she went a long time without blinking.
It's because I laughed at his story back then. I know it is.
This is only the beginning, isn't it.
Yes.

then.text: I thought of the sports field, where I was the only one who'd read that page properly; of the bathhouse door, where he'd said, "At least you read it to the end."
So that hadn't been nearly enough. I couldn't even change one person who wrote about a son turning into a pig.

commands.text: She pushed a sheet of paper into my hand. On it was her favourite story.
I don't believe in it any more. It isn't beautiful at all.
A few days later Liu Qingqing turned up at the cave mouth with a bag of bananas. We sat on the earth steps eating them.
That evening, I was coming back through the west gate and I saw Liang Xiao. Li Ning was following her, with three others. I hid behind a pile of bricks.
He didn't rape her. He took a pigskin out of his bag and made her take her clothes off and put it on.
Nobody chewed their banana any more.
I watched from behind the bricks. I never dared come out.
He ate three bananas in a row and kept eating. His eyes were full of hiding.

options.text: "Do you want to come and dig for gold?"
You can't find anything to say

commands.text: After that, Liu Qingqing stayed. He didn't go down into the hole much. He looked after the water, the food and the rubbish.
One night it was just him and me keeping watch at the cave mouth. Out of nowhere he started talking about his dad.
When my dad got drunk, he'd make me bring him a basin of hot water to wash his feet. From when I was ten until I was twenty.
Later he found a woman. I'd wash his feet, then he'd go and wash hers.
Funny, isn't it? One basin of water, and the whole family takes turns.
He laughed. I didn't. In the candlelight his round head looked like a bottle cap someone had screwed on too tight.
I hate him so much. …But whatever he tells me to do, I still do it.
I took the half-bag of bananas that was left and caught the bus into town to find Zhao Naifu.
He lived in a stone-paved alley. The chimney in his room came in through one window and went out through another.
That way you don't get gassed by the coal, and it heats the place too.
You weren't this clever before.
He took me for beef soup.

then.text: You know, at Shanchuan you're the only person who ever told me the truth. That wheelbarrow.

else.text: That wheelbarrow was from that house, wasn't it. …I knew all along. You even had to lie to me about that.

commands.text: I'm seeing a woman. She stays at mine at night, and I read to her.
She can't read?
She can't see.

Towards evening he came slowly towards me, leading a girl by the hand. Her eyes were large, clouded over with a greyish film. They walked that stretch of road very, very slowly. All at once I seemed to understand the pace Zhao Naifu lived at now.
I keep feeling it was me who ruined you.
Don't overthink it. You can't ruin anyone. People are very hard to change.
There's so much I can't figure out.
I've figured it all out.
His dogskin jacket disappeared into the far end of the lamplight. Waiting for the bus at the crossroads, I kept thinking: what had he figured out?
— 7 · War and Gold —
In late November, we dug up a wooden chest.
Thick poplar, half its paint gone, an old padlock hanging from it. It took two of us to carry it out. When we shook it, something rustled inside like dry straw.
Guo Zhonghan hit the lock a few times with the pickaxe. The lock held; the boards cracked first.
Stop smashing it. We can find the key.

options.text: Swing the pickaxe and break it open now

commands.text: The chest fell apart. Inside, on a bed of rotten straw, lay something made of bronze, rusted green.
It was a suit of armour. The edges had nearly rotted through; it looked as if it were dripping away bit by bit.
Ding Weiyang lifted it out and looked at it in the candlelight for a long time.
…Is this from ancient times?
Nobody answered him. We put the armour back and pushed the chest under Guo Zhonghan's camp bed.
The next day, Li Ning came walking towards the cave mouth with a dozen or so people. The moment Liu Qingqing saw him, he hid in the cave.
Li Ning's chin was covered in stubble as hard as nails, and his clothes were stiff as cardboard. He'd never wiped his hair again. I could smell petrol on them.
Tomorrow night, ten o'clock, in the square. Are you coming?
Ding Weiyang was leaning on his shovel. His eyebrows were darker than before, and sharper.
Why don't you just go and die?
Li Ning stared at him for a long time, then walked towards the cave.

You think you've been digging here two months and nobody knows? Everybody knows. Look north — there are eyes behind every one of those windows. From the first day they've watched you lot out here, playing make-believe. They've loved it.
I looked up. The glass in those low buildings to the north was catching the light.
From inside the cave came Liu Qingqing's shout, then the sound of wood being smashed.
Then a dozen people roaring with laughter. The laughter shook the whole tunnel until dirt pattered down from the roof.
They left. I could feel hundreds of eyes in the distant buildings, like scars burned into me one by one.
No digging today.
We blocked the cave mouth with the wheelbarrow.
In the canteen I smelled petrol again. I followed the smell round the back of the canteen: five brand-new iron drums with a bedsheet thrown over them.
I remembered what the hardware store owner had said: students from your school keep coming in for iron buckets, several at a time. So they'd already been preparing back then.
While we were still hesitating, several people came running at us. Yang Bang followed behind, breathing hard.
Anyone who knocks them over goes in one.

options.text: Get there first and kick a drum over

commands.prompt: Guo Zhonghan takes a step forward.

commands.text: I kicked. The drum went over, and the smell of petrol shot up like a flame, so strong I couldn't keep my eyes open.
Two of them picked up the drum that had rolled away and swung its base at my head. I heard my own teeth.
Guo Zhonghan hauled me up off the ground and stepped into the pool of petrol himself.
I grabbed Guo Zhonghan's arm. He shook me off and kicked a drum over.
Two of them picked it up and swung it down on his head.
Yang Bang jerked his chin towards the dorm block. On the third and fourth floors, window after window had been pushed open, and blank faces leaned out to watch us.
Guo Zhonghan got up off the ground, petrol dripping from his hair. He took out his lighter and flicked it on.
Guo Zhonghan.
Everything's so easy.
Yang Bang didn't move. Then he smiled, leaned in close to Guo Zhonghan, and said something quietly — something about Wang Ziye.
The flame flickered in Guo Zhonghan's hand, giving off a thin thread of black smoke.
Yang Bang turned and walked away. Someone stood the drum back up and pulled the bedsheet over it again.
That night in the cave, Guo Zhonghan said he ought to paint his face white, draw red circles on his cheeks, and run across the wasteland from east to west balancing on a ball.
You have to remember every second that you're a clown. If you forget, you can't go on living.
We slept the whole day away. There were footsteps in the corridor all day, and the clank of metal.
Towards evening we went back to the cave mouth and sat on the steps, looking at the dorm block in the distance. Every window was lit.

Ding Weiyang stood up and twisted his waist, and Liu Qingqing copied him. After a while Guo Zhonghan joined in. The three of them twisted back and forth in the dusk like three telegraph poles bent by the wind.
This feels so good. You should try it.
Why does it feel… kind of bleak to me?
At nine, a torch beam flashed across the square. On the horizon stood a dense crowd of silhouettes.
A ball of firelight came walking towards the cave mouth. Guo Zhonghan tightened his grip on his shovel.
When it came close, it was a girl with short hair, very pale skin, and lips that looked coated in a thin layer of ice.
I'm Liang Xiao's roommate. Before Liang Xiao left… she told me about you.
She planted her torch in the ground.
Let me dance for you.
The fog began to come down. She raised her arms and took small, quick steps.
In the distance, the first pane of glass broke. Someone was pushed out of a window. By the time the sounds reached us, they were as broken as a string of bells.

then.text: That chest… you remember what was inside it.
We watched her dance. Nobody answered.

else.text: Do you know what was in that chest? A suit of armour. A rotten suit of armour.
We watched her dance. Nobody answered.

commands.text: The first fireballs were thrown into the dorm block. Flames showed in the second-floor windows.
You should go.
The girl stopped, picked up her torch, and looked back towards the square.
Go where?
There was laughter everywhere. The Old Guard were laughing as they were beaten, laughing with their arms broken, laughter that could almost tear the walls apart.
From the cave came a clatter of metal.
Ding Weiyang walked out of the cave. He was wearing the bronze armour. The rotten plates came down over his eyebrows, and he carried a pickaxe.
Suddenly I remembered the joke from the seventh night. Not a scrap of armour left. We'd laughed all night — and the armour had been buried in our own hole the whole time.
There's no gold at all! There's nothing in this world!
He charged into the firelight with the pickaxe, the armour clattering like a long string of firecrackers.

I grabbed a shovel and followed. When I started running, my body felt so light it might take off. I hadn't run in a long time, and the feeling was almost happiness. That was the most frightening thing about that night.
Ding Weiyang swung the pickaxe into the arm of a man much bigger than him. The arm broke. The man fell to the ground, looked at his arm bent the wrong way, and laughed up at Ding Weiyang.
What the hell are you? Dressed up like that, who do you think you are?
Ding Weiyang froze. He'd never seen a laugh like that. Then he roared and stamped down.
In a corner of the square I saw the girl who had danced. She was crying.

then.text: An iron bar swung towards her. Without thinking, I blocked it with my shovel. The shock numbed my hands.

commands.text: What did Liang Xiao actually tell you?
She just cried.

Yang Bang stood in the middle of the crowd, a ring of people around him. Guo Zhonghan ran at him in a few strides and swung his shovel at Yang Bang's head — a kick came in from the side and caught him in the stomach. He dropped to his knees.
You're insane.
Do you think… you're great?
I am great. I did it. Tonight the bodies are everywhere.
I fended off someone lunging at me and grabbed Guo Zhonghan.
Come on, it's no use.
I can't stand it. …I'm a clown.
He shoved me down. The back of my head hit the ground.

then.text: I got up. He hadn't gone far. I threw myself at him again and locked my arms around his waist.
Guo Zhonghan struggled a couple of times and couldn't break free. He started crying in my arms, crying like a child who'd finally been allowed to.
Let go of me… let go…
In the distance, someone else set Yang Bang on fire. The flames lit up Guo Zhonghan's face. He didn't turn to look.

else.text: By the time I got up, Guo Zhonghan had thrown a bottle of petrol over Yang Bang and tossed the lighter after it.
I'm a despicable man! I'm a saint!
Yang Bang went up in flames. He screamed and tore at his clothes, but tearing them off didn't help any more.

The last time I saw Guo Zhonghan, a new student whose face he'd slashed got up from the foot of the wall, swung a shovel and brought it down on the back of his head. As he fell, the corner of his mouth still held that smile — the same smile as when he'd said "These people are hilarious" in the canteen.

commands.text: Outside the canteen, Liu Qingqing had Li Ning by the throat.
Where's your pigskin? I'll kill you!
Li Ning ground his cigarette into Liu Qingqing's wrist. Liu Qingqing didn't let go at all, as if that hand no longer belonged to him. Locked together, they rolled down the steps.
I remembered what he'd said in the candlelight: whatever he tells me to do, I still do it. This time, nobody had told him to.
The last time I saw Ding Weiyang, a few people were stripping the armour off him and putting it on themselves piece by piece, shouting at the night sky: "I'm different now!"
Blood was seeping out from inside the bronze plates. Ding Weiyang probably didn't know where he was hurt either.

then.text: He recognised me. Without the armour, his thick black eyebrows showed again.
That night… you came at them.
He'd only said that much before the crowd swept him away.

else.text: He recognised me. Without the armour, his thick black eyebrows showed again, and his eyes were full of a sorrow there was no end to.
It was exactly the look from the seventh night. That night, too, I had only stood in the doorway and watched.

commands.text: I went back into the cave and lit every candle.
The sounds outside came through dozens of metres of earth: laughter, breaking glass, the clatter of metal. After a while I couldn't make anything out, only my own heartbeat.
I told myself: this has nothing to do with us. We're only here to dig for gold.
Just before dawn, someone came feeling their way into the cave in the dark. It was the girl who had danced, her face grey with ash.
You've been here the whole time?
Yes.
…None of them came back.
She sat down at the edge of the camp bed. Neither of us said anything more.
After that, I was put in charge of guarding the five petrol drums behind the canteen.
Those five iron drums were brand new and shiny. I recognised them: the same kind the hardware store had sold out of. So I'd been standing on this side all along; I just hadn't known it yet.
One day Guo Zhonghan and the others came round the back. When Guo Zhonghan saw me, he froze.
You're guarding their petrol?
Anyone who knocks them over goes in one.
Guo Zhonghan kicked a drum over.

options.text: You pick up a drum too

commands.prompt: Petrol spreads across the ground. The man next to you picks up the drum that rolled away.

commands.text: The base of a drum smashed into Guo Zhonghan's head. He fell into the petrol, got up again, and took out his lighter.
Yang Bang wasn't afraid at all. Smiling, he leaned in and said something about Wang Ziye.
The flame trembled in Guo Zhonghan's hand for a long time, and finally went out.
At ten that night I stood in the square with a steel pipe in my hand.
The second-floor windows broke one after another. Fireballs were thrown in. The Old Guard jumped out of the windows and we chased them and beat them.
They were laughing. Laughing with their arms broken. I didn't understand what they were laughing at.
When I swung the first blow, I wasn't thinking anything. The second, the third — the same.
In the distance, someone in bronze armour charged into the crowd with a pickaxe, the plates clattering. It was Ding Weiyang.
"There's no gold at all!" he shouted.
Not a scrap of armour left. I remembered the joke, but I couldn't laugh at all.
I saw Guo Zhonghan throw a bottle of petrol over Yang Bang. When Yang Bang went up in flames, Wang Ziye ran away screaming.
Later, someone stripped the armour off Ding Weiyang piece by piece. A bronze plate fell at my feet, still bloody.

options.text: Drop the steel pipe and walk south towards the cave

commands.prompt: The bronze plate glints in the firelight.

commands.text: I pressed the plate to my chest and shouted at the night sky:
I'm different now!
Everyone around me was shouting too. The shouting and the laughter mixed together and poured off into some crack deep in the wasteland.
After dawn, police cars came along the highway, one after another.
Many years later I still have that bronze plate. It stopped shining long ago; it's as green as a patch of moss.
I never went into that cave. I don't know how far down they dug in the end.
All I know is that on that night, I turned into something too.
【Ending: I'm Different Now】
My shoulder was dislocated and my knee was hurt. I dragged my feet back.

People carried the injured out into the wasteland in pairs, just as Yang Bang had planned, except nobody could tell who they were carrying. Lord Westgate carried the wounded on his back by himself, dozens of them. As he went up the canteen steps, I heard a dull thud behind me. I didn't look back. For a long time, I didn't dare look back.
In the small hours, the fog swallowed everything. Going by feel, I limped back to the cave.
I lit a candle and looked at my wounds. For some reason I was glad to be alive. Apart from being alive, I finally didn't want anything at all.
Ten minutes later, someone stood up in the corner. It was the girl who had danced.
Dance for me.
She wiped her eyes and shook her head.
— 8 · Leaving —
For a long time after that, I didn't leave the cave.
Under the camp bed I found Ding Weiyang's notebook. The first pages had been torn out down to ragged edges, used up by other people writing their stories. On the last page there were three lines:
Today I am very happy
Today we dug one metre
Today I am not weak any more
After that, nothing.
During the day the girl would bring me food. I didn't know whether the school was still there.

She read me the Bible. She said people like me were full of sin, that I had to repent, had to pray. There was one line she read that sounded familiar — the one copied on my locker door, about the earth being filled with violence. I just looked at her. All that sin and punishment she talked about became beautiful, like her.
Dig for gold with me.
She picked up the shovel I'd washed clean, stood in the candlelight, and suddenly laughed out loud.
This is so wrong. I can't believe in it.
She hung a little cross at the head of the camp bed.
When it's hard, talk to it. It'll get better.
Then where was it before all this?
She had no answer. About a week later she left, and never came back.

then.text: Ding Weiyang and Liu Qingqing never came back. Guo Zhonghan came once. He stood at the cave mouth and didn't come in.
I'm going home. …I've got a bad feeling about this.
He gave a little smile, put a packet of cigarettes on the step, and left. I hoped that this time, too, his bad feeling would come true.

else.text: Ding Weiyang, Guo Zhonghan, Liu Qingqing — none of them ever came back.

Later, on the highway, I saw a familiar back through the window of a bus, and couldn't tell whether it was Ding Weiyang, or Guo Zhonghan, or Liu Qingqing. The bus was going too fast for me to be sure. Maybe I didn't want to be sure.

then.text: I often dream about the moments when I looked away. In the dreams, I never once turn back.

commands.text: A month later, Zhao Naifu turned up at the cave mouth with a bag of bananas.
I'm a pimp now. She's with me.
What are you going to do?
What are you going to do?
I'm fine.
I've decided. I'm not sharing the gold with anyone. None of you know what can save you.
Keep it. Nobody needs gold. …If you can't go on, come and find me in town.
You're a traitor. I'm not coming to find you.
One summer I went back to the abandoned dorm. The windows were blackened by the fire on the second floor. Under a mattress, I found the plank.
The words hadn't changed at all; they'd just dried out. I hung it next to the cross. One said you will be saved, the other said you have no one to lean on, and every day I slept between them.
That was when it suddenly came back to me: that day on the wasteland, there hadn't been just one rock. What was under the other two?
I didn't plan to turn them over before I found the gold. I was afraid that once I did, there'd be no possibility left.
In the winter of the fourth year, the pickaxe made a different sound.
I knelt in the candlelight for a long time. Then I carefully chipped off a piece the size of a fingernail with the pickaxe and put it in my pocket.
At last I could leave this place.
The town had changed. New buildings had gone up, and the glass on that street wasn't held together with tape any more.
I exchanged the little piece of gold for money. Behind a brand-new pane of glass, I saw the girl who had danced.
The ice on her lips had melted.
I gave her all the money. She stayed with me for a night.
I haven't slept indoors for four years.
You're the one who was digging for gold. …Did you find any?
What do you think?
You were just killing time, weren't you?
Maybe.
I'd like to see what a huge pile of gold looks like.
It's nothing much. Without candles, it's just a dark mass.
In the winter of the fourth year, the pickaxe struck rock.
I tried three directions. All rock. Under this whole wasteland there was one solid slab of stone.
This was where the cave ended. I sat in the candlelight and burned the last candle down.
I went into town. New buildings had gone up, and the glass on that street wasn't held together with tape any more.
Behind a brand-new pane of glass, I saw the girl who had danced. The ice on her lips had melted.
You're the one who was digging for gold. …Did you find any?
No.
She chewed a strand of her hair and looked at me for a long time.
Then what were you doing all those four years?
Digging.
She laughed, just like that day in the cave.
That night I asked you what Liang Xiao told you. You never said.
She thought for a while, as if searching for something put away a long time ago.
She said that in this whole school, only those few digging the hole in the south were still doing anything.
She said she wanted to know what would become of people like that in the end. But she couldn't wait to find out.
So I went to dance for you. To see it for her.
And did you see?
I did. …It was nothing much.
I went back to the cave and buried the pots and pans. Ding Weiyang's notebook I put inside my coat.
I was never coming back to this hole. That night, before crossing the mountains, there was a goodness to it I can't describe.
But there was still an empty place in me. Might there be something better under the other two rocks?
I still hadn't found the answer. I had only lived through four years.

options.text: Go to the village in the north
Go east and turn over the other two rocks

commands.text: I walked to the gate of that house, circled the yard wall once, and climbed over.
In the yard, a flock of white silkie chickens wandered free. The very ones from my dream.
By the wall was a box of candles, thick with dust, not one of them touched. Next to it leaned a new pickaxe, the eye that couldn't close carved into its handle.
A little boy was crouching on the ground, holding a fistful of yellow earth.
Who are you?
I shook my head.
Are you a thief?
Yes.
A sadness I had never felt before seized me. For more than a thousand days and nights I had never let go, and now I couldn't hold it back at all.
The man who had lost his pickaxe came out of the house, looked at me, and smiled faintly. He glanced at the candles by the wall, then back at me. He had known all along.
I stole your pickaxe.
The man and the boy both looked at me.
Let me dance for you.
Remembering, as best I could, the short-haired girl, I spread my arms.
【Ending: I Stole Your Pickaxe】
The hut was still there. On the side of the first rock we had turned over, the moss had long since dried.
I went to the second rock, crouched, and set my shoulder against it.
It was lighter than I remembered. When it turned over, underneath was a shallow hollow with nothing in it but a few white feathers.
I went to the third rock. When I turned it over, there was a plank under it too.
The plank was new. There wasn't a single word on it.
I sat beside it for a long time. The wind swam over the tips of the grass like a shoal of fish.
Then I picked up a sharp stone and carved words into the plank. I carved slowly, crookedly, just like that person all those years ago.
When I'd finished, I put the plank back in the hollow, turned the rock back over, and pressed it down.
I don't know who will be the next to lift it. Maybe, many years from now, another young person who doesn't know what to do with himself.
I only hope the words he sees are different from the ones I saw.

then.text: I set off towards the town. Zhao Naifu had said that if I couldn't go on, I could come and find him. I can go on. I just want to see him.

else.text: I walked towards the highway. A bus came, and I got on without asking where it was going.

commands.text: 【Ending: The Other Two Stones】
